text: What does 'PII' stand for?
options: Personally Identifiable Information
Public Internal Information
Personal Internet Identity
Protected Internal Index
explanation: PII is any information that can identify a specific person, such as a name, address, or ID number.

text: Which of these is the safest place to keep a work password?
options: A password manager
A sticky note on your monitor
A shared spreadsheet
A text file named 'passwords.txt'
explanation: A password manager stores credentials securely and encrypted, unlike sticky notes or plain text files.

text: You get an urgent email from an unknown sender asking you to click a link to 'verify your account'. What should you do first?
options: Click the link immediately
Check the sender's real address and hover over the link before doing anything
Forward it to a friend
Reply asking for more details
explanation: Checking the sender and the real destination of a link is the first step in spotting phishing attempts.

text: Which data classification is meant for absolutely anyone to see?
options: Restricted
Confidential
Internal
Public
explanation: Public data is meant for anyone; sharing it causes no harm.

text: What is the main purpose of Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)?
options: To make logging in slower for no reason
To add a second layer of proof beyond just a password
To replace passwords entirely
To track your location
explanation: MFA requires a second proof of identity, so a stolen password alone is not enough to log in.

text: You find a USB drive in the parking lot at work. What should you do?
options: Plug it into your work computer to see what's on it
Give it to IT or security without plugging it in
Take it home
Give it to a random colleague
explanation: Unknown USB drives can carry malware. Let IT or security inspect it safely.

text: Which of the following is an example of a strong password practice?
options: Using the same password everywhere
Using a long, unique passphrase for each account
Using 'Password123'
Writing your password in your email signature
explanation: Long, unique passphrases per account limit the damage if one account is ever breached.

text: What should you do when you leave your desk, even for a few minutes?
options: Leave your screen unlocked so you can get back quickly
Lock your screen
Turn off the monitor only
Log out of email only
explanation: Locking your screen prevents anyone from using your session while you're away.

text: Why should you avoid discussing confidential work matters in public places like a train?
options: It's rude
Someone nearby could overhear sensitive information
It uses too much data
It's against etiquette rules only
explanation: Eavesdroppers in public places are a real and easy way for sensitive information to leak.

text: What is 'phishing'?
options: A legitimate IT support process
An attempt to trick you into revealing sensitive information or clicking malicious links
A method to speed up your email
A type of firewall
explanation: Phishing uses deceptive messages to trick people into giving up information or access.

text: Which of these is personal data?
options: A company's stock price
An employee's home address
The office holiday calendar
A published price list
explanation: A home address identifies and locates a specific person, so it is personal data.

text: What should you do with printed documents containing confidential information when you're done with them?
options: Leave them on your desk
Put them in a regular recycling bin
Shred them or use a secure disposal bin
Give them to a colleague
explanation: Shredding or secure disposal prevents confidential paperwork from being read by the wrong people.

text: Why is a 'clean desk policy' important?
options: It just looks tidy
It reduces the risk of sensitive documents being seen or taken by unauthorized people
It saves paper
It's required by fire code
explanation: An empty desk means no sensitive papers are left exposed to visitors or cleaning staff.

text: What does 'least privilege' mean in data access?
options: Giving everyone full access to be helpful
Giving people only the access they need to do their job
Giving no one any access
Giving temporary staff more access than employees
explanation: Least privilege limits exposure: if an account is compromised, the damage is limited to what it could access.

text: Which of these is the best way to share a sensitive file with a colleague?
options: Post it on a public forum
Use an approved, secure company system
Email it to your personal email first
Print it and leave it on their desk
explanation: Approved company systems are set up with the right access controls and protections.

text: What is the safest thing to do about a suspicious email?
options: Reply and ask if it's legitimate
Report it to IT or security using the official process
Forward it to all your friends as a joke
Open every attachment to check it
explanation: Reporting through official channels lets security investigate without risking further exposure.

text: What is a VPN mainly used for?
options: Speeding up your internet
Creating a secure, encrypted connection over a public network
Blocking all cookies
Backing up your files
explanation: A VPN encrypts your traffic, protecting it especially on untrusted networks like public Wi-Fi.

text: Which of these is a sign of a phishing email?
options: It's from a colleague you email daily with no unusual request
Urgent language, spelling mistakes, and a mismatched sender address
It has the company logo
It arrived during work hours
explanation: Urgency, poor spelling, and mismatched sender details are classic phishing red flags.

text: What should you do before doing work on public Wi-Fi?
options: Just connect - it's fine
Use a VPN or avoid handling sensitive data on it
Turn off your firewall for better speed
Share the Wi-Fi password with others
explanation: Public Wi-Fi can be monitored by others nearby, so sensitive work should go through a VPN.

text: Why do companies label data as 'Confidential' or 'Restricted'?
options: To make files feel important
So everyone knows how carefully that information must be handled
It's a marketing tactic
It has no real purpose
explanation: Classification labels tell people exactly how much care and protection a piece of data needs.

text: What should you do if you accidentally send a sensitive file to the wrong person?
options: Ignore it and hope no one notices
Report it immediately so it can be addressed
Ask the recipient to keep it secret
Delete it from your sent folder and move on
explanation: Quick reporting lets the security team limit the damage, such as revoking access or notifying people.

text: Which of these is the best example of a strong password?
options: qwerty123
Tr0ubl3-Kite-Lamp!92
password
Your pet's name
explanation: Long, random-looking passphrases are much harder to guess or crack than common words.

text: What is a 'data breach'?
options: A scheduled software update
When sensitive data is accessed or exposed without authorization
A backup process
A type of firewall rule
explanation: A breach is any unauthorized access to or exposure of sensitive data.

text: Why should work laptops be encrypted?
options: It makes the laptop faster
So data can't be read if the laptop is lost or stolen
It's required for warranty
It reduces file size
explanation: Disk encryption keeps data unreadable to anyone who doesn't have the right key or password, even with the physical drive in hand.

text: A colleague asks you to share your login credentials so they can 'quickly check something'. What should you do?
options: Share it, they're a colleague
Refuse, and offer to get them proper access through official channels
Share it but change your password later
Ask your manager first, then share anyway
explanation: Credentials should never be shared; proper access should always go through official channels.

text: Which classification would a signed customer contract with pricing terms usually fall under?
options: Public
Internal
Confidential
It doesn't need a classification
explanation: Contracts often carry confidentiality clauses and sensitive terms, so they are typically Confidential.

text: What's the real difference between 'Internal' and 'Confidential' data?
options: There is no difference
Internal is for anyone outside the company; Confidential is for staff only
Internal is for employees generally; Confidential needs stricter protection due to higher harm if leaked
Confidential is less sensitive than Internal
explanation: Both stay inside the company, but Confidential data causes real harm if it leaks, so it needs stronger controls.

text: What is 'social engineering'?
options: Building workplace friendships
Manipulating people into breaking security procedures or giving up information
A type of encryption
A HR training program
explanation: Social engineering targets people, not systems, tricking them into giving up access or information.

text: Why is it risky to post a photo of your work badge or ID on social media?
options: It's not risky at all
It could help someone impersonate you or forge access credentials
It uses too much bandwidth
It violates dress code
explanation: Badge photos can reveal details attackers use to create fake credentials or impersonate staff.

text: What should happen to a hard drive before it is thrown away or recycled?
options: Nothing, just throw it out
It should be securely wiped or physically destroyed
Format it once with a quick format
Remove the sticker with the serial number
explanation: A quick format doesn't erase the underlying data; secure wiping or physical destruction is needed.

text: Why might GPS location data embedded in a photo be a privacy concern?
options: It makes photos larger
It can unintentionally reveal someone's location or other private details
It slows down file transfer
It has no relation to privacy
explanation: Photo metadata can quietly leak where and when a picture was taken.

text: What is 'data minimization'?
options: Compressing files to save space
Collecting and keeping only the personal data that's actually necessary
Deleting all data regularly regardless of need
Reducing the number of employees who can see any data
explanation: Data minimization reduces risk by only collecting and retaining what is genuinely needed.

text: An external vendor asks for a large export of customer data 'just in case they need it later'. What's the appropriate response?
options: Send it right away to be helpful
Provide only what's needed for the agreed purpose, following data-sharing procedures
Ignore the request
Ask the vendor to send you their own database first
explanation: Data should only be shared for its agreed purpose, following the proper approval process.

text: Why is 'segregation of duties' used for sensitive processes like payroll?
options: To slow things down on purpose
So no single person has enough control to commit fraud or errors unnoticed
Because one person can't be trusted ever
It's only a tradition, not a safeguard
explanation: Splitting responsibilities makes it much harder for a single person to misuse a sensitive process undetected.

text: What is the risk of using the same password across multiple accounts?
options: None, if the password is long
If one account is breached, attackers can access all your other accounts with that password
It's more convenient and therefore safer
Passwords can't be reused technically
explanation: Reused passwords mean one leak can compromise every account that shares it.

text: Why should test or development environments avoid using real customer data unmasked?
options: Real data is more accurate for testing
Test environments often have weaker security, so real data there increases exposure risk
It's slower to load real data
There's no reason, it's just convention
explanation: Lower-security test systems are a common place for real sensitive data to leak if it isn't masked first.

text: What should you check before clicking a link in an email asking you to log in?
options: Nothing, links are usually safe
That the link actually points to the real, expected domain (hover to check)
That the email has a logo
That the email was sent during business hours
explanation: Hovering over a link reveals its real destination, which phishing emails often disguise.

text: Why is 'tailgating' (following someone through a secure door without badging in) a security risk?
options: It's just impolite
It lets unauthorized people bypass physical access controls
It slows down the door
It's not actually a risk
explanation: Tailgating defeats badge-based access control, letting anyone slip into secure areas.

text: What does 'encryption at rest' protect against?
options: Data being unreadable while being typed
Unauthorized access to data while it's stored on disk
Slow internet speeds
Data being deleted
explanation: Encryption at rest protects stored data, so it stays unreadable even if the storage is accessed directly.

text: You need to email a spreadsheet classified as 'Restricted'. What should you do?
options: Email it as normal, restricted just means important
Follow the approved secure method for restricted data (e.g. encrypted transfer, need-to-know recipients only)
Rename the file so it looks less sensitive
Post it on the internal wiki for convenience
explanation: Restricted data needs the strongest handling: encrypted transfer and only named, approved recipients.

text: What's a good reason to use a password manager?
options: It shares your passwords with your team automatically
It lets you use long, unique passwords for every account without memorizing them
It removes the need for MFA
It backs up your files to the cloud
explanation: Password managers make strong, unique passwords practical to use everywhere.

text: Why should you verify a caller's identity before discussing account details, even if they claim to be from IT?
options: Because IT never calls
Because attackers sometimes impersonate IT or other trusted staff to extract information
Because phone calls are always recorded
There's no need if they know your name
explanation: Impersonating trusted staff (pretexting) is a common social engineering tactic.

text: What's the risk of 'shadow IT' (using unapproved apps or tools for work data)?
options: There is no risk if the app is popular
It can bypass company security controls, so data may not be protected as expected
It's always faster and better
IT prefers you find your own tools
explanation: Unapproved tools haven't been vetted, so company data inside them may not be properly protected.

text: Why do companies set data retention periods (how long data is kept)?
options: To fill up storage on purpose
Keeping data only as long as needed reduces risk and meets legal requirements
Retention periods are arbitrary and have no benefit
To make audits harder
explanation: Data that no longer needs to exist is data that can't be stolen; retention limits reduce that risk.

text: A pop-up claims your computer is infected and gives a phone number to call for 'support'. What is this most likely?
options: A legitimate antivirus alert
A scam (tech support scam) trying to trick you into giving access or payment
A normal Windows update
Nothing to worry about
explanation: Tech support scams use scary pop-ups to pressure people into giving remote access or money.

text: Why is anonymized data generally lower risk than data with names attached?
options: Anonymized data is always public
Removing identifying details makes it much harder to link the data back to a specific person
Anonymization has no effect on risk
Anonymized data is always fake
explanation: Without identifying details, it's much harder to connect a record back to one real person.

text: A coworker is being asked by someone else to share their password. What should you do?
options: Mind your own business
Point out that credentials should never be shared and suggest the proper process
Share your own password too, to help
Report the coworker to HR immediately
explanation: Speaking up about credential sharing helps prevent a common and risky mistake.

text: Why is it important to log off shared or public computers after use?
options: It isn't necessary if you close the browser
Being logged in leaves your account accessible to whoever uses the computer next
It only matters for personal computers
Logging off deletes your account
explanation: Closing the browser doesn't always end a session; logging off explicitly does.

text: A partner company wants read-only access to a shared folder that mixes project files with some Confidential HR documents. What's the best practice?
options: Grant access to the whole folder since it's just read-only
Separate the Confidential documents into a different location before granting any external access
It's fine since read-only can't be misused
Ask the partner to promise not to look at HR files
explanation: Access should be scoped to only what's needed; mixed folders should be split before external access is granted.

text: Which scenario best shows 'need-to-know' being violated, even though no data was leaked?
options: A finance employee accesses the salary database to process payroll
A curious employee with no work reason browses colleagues' salary records they technically have access to
An HR employee reviews benefits enrollment forms
A manager reviews their own team's leave requests
explanation: Having access isn't the same as having a reason; browsing without a work need breaks need-to-know even without a leak.

text: A dataset has names removed but keeps date of birth, zip code, and gender for each record. Why might this still be risky?
options: It's completely safe once names are removed
Combining a few indirect details like these can often re-identify a specific person
Dates of birth are considered fake data
Zip codes are never linked to identity
explanation: Quasi-identifiers like birth date, zip code, and gender can combine to uniquely identify most people.

text: An employee considers pasting a confidential client contract into a new AI writing assistant to get a summary. What's the concern?
options: There is no concern, it's just software
Pasting confidential data into an unapproved external tool may send that data outside company control
AI tools always delete inputs immediately
Only images are risky to share with AI tools
explanation: Unapproved external tools may store, log, or reuse whatever data is entered, so confidential data shouldn't go in.

text: An access log shows an employee viewed a customer record at 2am from an unusual location. On its own, is this proof of a data breach?
options: Yes, always
Not necessarily - it's a red flag worth investigating, not proof of wrongdoing by itself
No, log times are never accurate
It's only concerning if the data was deleted
explanation: Unusual activity is a signal to investigate, not automatic proof of a breach.

text: Why can metadata about communications (who talked to whom, when, how often) still be sensitive, even without message content?
options: Metadata is never sensitive
Patterns of contact can reveal relationships, investigations, or sensitive activity even without content
Metadata is only used for billing
It only matters for phone companies
explanation: Contact patterns alone can expose sensitive relationships or activities, even with no message content visible.

text: A vendor asks for production customer data to help 'debug an issue faster'. What's the more secure alternative?
options: Send the full production dataset since it's urgent
Provide masked or synthetic data, or the minimum real data needed under a data-sharing agreement
Ask the vendor to sign an NDA and then send everything
There is no safer alternative
explanation: Masked or synthetic data, or the minimum necessary real data, limits exposure while still enabling debugging.

text: What's the biggest risk of classifying data as 'Confidential' when it should really be 'Restricted'?
options: None, over-classifying is always safer
Under-classifying it means it won't get the stronger protections it actually needs, increasing breach risk
Only fines depend on classification, not actual risk
Classification labels don't affect how data is handled
explanation: Under-classified data is handled with weaker safeguards than it actually requires.

text: A former employee's main account is deactivated on their last day, but a personal phone app they connected months earlier still holds an active API token. What's the risk?
options: None - deactivating the main account is always enough
Lingering tokens or integrations can retain access even after the main account is disabled, unless separately revoked
API tokens expire automatically within a day
Personal apps can never access company data
explanation: Connected apps and tokens often need to be revoked separately from the main account.

text: Why is encryption in transit alone not sufficient to protect a file shared via a cloud link set to 'anyone with the link'?
options: It is always sufficient
Once opened, the decrypted content is accessible to anyone who has the link, regardless of transit encryption
Encryption in transit prevents all possible access
Cloud links can't be encrypted
explanation: Transit encryption protects data on the way, but an overly open sharing link exposes the content once it's opened.

text: Which best describes 'pretexting' in a social engineering attack?
options: Sending random spam emails
Creating a fabricated scenario or false identity to convince someone to share information or grant access
Guessing passwords repeatedly
Installing malware via USB
explanation: Pretexting relies on a believable but fake story to manipulate someone into helping the attacker.

text: 'Internal' data is shareable with all employees. An employee posts an internal report to a public online forum to get outside advice. What's wrong here?
options: Nothing, it's not Public data so slightly wider sharing is fine
'Internal' means for employees only - sharing it externally breaks the classification's intent, even to a public forum
Public forums are considered internal to the company
Only Confidential and Restricted data have sharing restrictions
explanation: Internal data is bounded by the company; posting it externally, anywhere, breaks that boundary.

text: Two datasets are each individually anonymized and released by different teams. Why could combining them still create a privacy risk?
options: Combining anonymized datasets is always safe
Cross-referencing multiple anonymized sources can sometimes re-identify individuals that neither dataset alone would reveal
Anonymized datasets cannot technically be combined
This is only a risk for financial data
explanation: Combining separate anonymized sources can expose identities that were safe in each dataset alone.

text: Why do security policies often require periodically reviewing user access rights, not just at hire and termination?
options: It's just a bureaucratic formality with no real value
People's roles change over time, and unused or outdated permissions can accumulate into unnecessary risk
It's required only for new employees
Access rights never change once granted
explanation: Access recertification catches 'access creep' - old permissions that outlived their reason.

text: A Restricted document is password-protected and emailed, with the password sent in a later email to the same recipient. What's the main weakness?
options: There is no weakness, this is best practice
If the email account or a shared mailbox is compromised, both the file and its password may be exposed through the same channel
Passwords should never be typed twice
Emails cannot carry attachments larger than 1MB
explanation: Sending both the file and its password through the same channel defeats the point of a separate password.

text: Why might a company classify aggregated, anonymous survey results as Internal rather than Public, even though no individual can be identified?
options: Aggregation always makes data Public automatically
The results may still reveal competitively sensitive business information, even without personal data involved
Anonymous data legally must always be Internal
There's no valid reason; it should always be Public
explanation: Classification also protects business sensitivity, not just personal privacy.

text: An employee gets a legitimate-looking invoice email urgently asking to change a supplier's bank details before payment. What should they do?
options: Update the bank details immediately to avoid a late payment
Verify the change through a separate, trusted channel before acting, since this is a common fraud pattern
Reply to the email asking for confirmation
Forward the invoice to accounts payable without any checks
explanation: This is a classic business email compromise pattern; always verify payment changes out-of-band.

text: Why is understanding where data travels (systems, vendors, backups) important for classification to actually work?
options: It isn't important, classification only matters at creation
A classification is only as strong as its weakest link; data can end up in less-protected systems if flows aren't tracked
Data flow only matters for network engineers
Classification automatically follows data everywhere with no tracking needed
explanation: Protection can quietly weaken if data flows into systems that don't honor the original classification.

text: A dataset replaces names with sequential ID numbers, but the original name-to-ID mapping is kept in the same file on a different tab. Is this dataset properly anonymized?
options: Yes, because names are removed from the main data
No - this is pseudonymization, not anonymization, since the mapping still allows re-identification
Yes, as long as the tab is hidden
It depends only on the file format
explanation: Keeping a mapping back to identities means the data is only pseudonymized, not truly anonymized.

text: Why do breach notification rules typically require reporting incidents involving personal data within a set timeframe?
options: To generate bad publicity for companies
So affected individuals and regulators can respond quickly to reduce harm
It's purely a tax reporting requirement
These laws only apply to breaches of Public data
explanation: Fast notification lets people take protective action, like changing passwords or watching for fraud.

text: A manager asks a former team member to keep sharing sensitive project data after they've moved to a different team with no continuing need. What should the employee do, per 'need-to-know'?
options: Keep sharing indefinitely since it's their old manager
Politely decline and suggest the manager request access through the proper channel if there's a genuine ongoing need
Share it once more and then stop
Ask HR to fire the manager
explanation: Need-to-know applies regardless of past relationships; access should follow a current, genuine need.

text: Why can leftover local copies of a Restricted file (in a temp folder, email draft, or sync client) undermine an otherwise strong access control policy?
options: Local copies are always automatically encrypted the same as the original
These extra copies may not inherit the same access restrictions or get deleted when the original is revoked, creating hidden exposure
Temp folders are inaccessible to anyone, including the file owner
This is not a real concern in practice
explanation: Stray local copies can silently outlive the access controls or deletion of the original file.
